beats: Hook: her slide (Q25-07 s14, 15:31-16:24) puts |+> through the matrix Z twice. As a gate, Z turns |+> into |-> (one definite new state, nothing random, and a second Z undoes it); as a measurement, Z turns |+> into 0 or 1 with odds 1/2 each, and nothing undoes it. Same matrix: a flick or a slap (line_qc_meas_flick_or_slap, then the cover). FACT CHECK: the syllabus hook says the gate 'leaves |+> untouched' and the machine transcript at Q25-07 16:05 says 'it will be still a plus': Z|+> = |->. Never clip 16:03-16:11; 'totally different' is clean at 15:31-15:45 and 16:11-16:24 (check by ear).

The only window (clip Q25-07 02:59-03:25): everything we ever learn from a quantum computer comes out as measurement results; nothing else leaves the box (line_qc_meas_sealed_cabinet). Cast for all of QC06: the experimenter (spiky hair, goggles pushed up, lab coat) and the traveller (tall, curly hair, knitted beanie, padded jacket, messenger bag); props: the reading box (two round lamps = the two outcomes) and the coin with a daisy face.

Why measurements are Hermitian matrices: what nature hands us is a real reading, a needle on a dial, never a complex number (clip Q24-08 02:24-02:52; reuse line_postal_scale). Hermitian matrices have real eigenvalues (the short proof, Q25-07 03:49-09:29, Q24-08.notes p1); the possible readings are the eigenvalues: +1 and -1 for Z.

A projector is a shadow (Q24-08 15:38-16:36): the arrow's shadow on the floor under a lamp straight above; an arrow already lying on the floor casts exactly itself, so projecting twice is projecting once, P^2 = P (line_qc_meas_shadow_twice).

Born rule (12:37-15:31): each reading is random; its odds are the squared length of the shadow, |<0|psi>|^2. One run shows one lamp; odds show only by repeating the run on fresh copies and counting (line_qc_meas_bead_jars: two even jars for |+>; line_qc_meas_bead_jars_tilted: a tilted arrow, about 4 to 1). The average reading is <Z> = (+1)p0 + (-1)p1 = <psi|Z|psi>. Any arrow goes in, only one of two answers comes out (reuse line_switch_dimmer: a switch, not a dimmer; reuse line_dice_hand for the randomness).
After the reading the state is the eigenvector that was read: a slapped coin stays slapped; read it again and you get the same answer (line_qc_meas_flick_or_slap, right half).

X measurement = H, then Z measurement (16:51-23:36, Q25-07 s16, Q24-08 28:51-31:31): H turns the X-basis states into the Z-basis states, so the camera stays bolted to the floor and you turn the object instead (line_qc_meas_fixed_camera).

Why it matters (clip Q25-07 18:16-18:42): hardware calibrates one measurement well and builds every other one from gates, as it calibrates one two-qubit gate and builds the rest (line_qc_meas_one_box_calm); the general recipe: any measurement = a unitary, then Z measurements (Q24-08 34:10-35:04). Tape Q25-07 s16 and Q24-08.notes p3.
Takeaway: a gate is an action you can undo; a measurement is a question whose answer replaces the state. Next: asking two qubits one question (QC06-02). Avoid Q24-08 32:39-33:05 (quiz logistics).
Cover (line_qc_cover_06_01; for the X post and thumbnails, not a film beat): the experimenter flicks one spinning coin and slaps another flat.
